Pool repair in Yuma usually begins with one small sign: the water line sits lower on the tile, a crack shows up in the plaster, or the light stays dark after sunset. Each one can be minor or the start of something larger, and the only way to know is to find the cause before anyone replaces parts.

This page covers repairs to the pool itself: its shell and finish, the plumbing and fittings, skimmers, lights, tile and drain covers. Equipment pad problems have their own pages: pool pump repair, and filter, heater and salt cell repair.

A note on who does what: Yuma Pool Cleaning Pro is only a free phone connection and never touches a pool. After you explain the problem, your call is handed to an independent Yuma-area pool company. That company inspects, prices the job itself and carries out the repair.

Leak or evaporation? Yuma makes it hard to tell

Every pool loses water to the air, and Yuma's weather speeds that up: National Weather Service normals give Yuma roughly 118 days of 100 degree heat or more each year. EPA WaterSense says a typical uncovered pool can lose 12,000 to 31,000 gallons a year to evaporation, depending on where it is, and that a cover can stop up to 95 percent of that loss.

So a falling water level is not proof of a leak. EPA WaterSense gives a rule of thumb: losing more than 2 inches a week, or more than 3 inches a week in hot, dry areas, suggests a leak. Higher water bills, wet soil near the pool and an auto fill that seems to run all the time are other clues.

The bucket test: a safe check you can do

  1. Pick a calm day with no rain in the forecast. Turn off the pump, any cleaner and the automatic fill, and keep everyone out of the pool.
  2. Fill a bucket with pool water to about an inch below the rim. Set it on the first step so most of the bucket sits under the pool's surface.
  3. Draw a line at the water surface inside the bucket, and put a piece of tape on the tile at the pool's surface.
  4. After 24 hours, measure both drops. If the pool fell more than the bucket, the pool is probably losing water somewhere besides the air.

The bucket test tells you whether there is a leak. It does not tell you where it is. EPA WaterSense also suggests repeating a manual leak test every few months and making sure an automatic fill valve shuts off properly.

Where pool leaks usually hide

EPA WaterSense lists the usual places a pool loses water: the shell or liner, the pump seal, the pipes, the point where a pipe meets the pool, the pool edges and the pipe joints. Skimmers, return fittings, the main drain and the seals around lights are all connection points of that kind. Wet or sunken soil between the pool and the equipment can point toward a buried pipe.

Finding the exact spot is a job for professional leak detection. Angi's leak detection guide describes a pressure test of the lines as a common first step, because it can narrow down a leak without digging, and treats digging up the yard as a last resort once other tests have failed.

Before anyone drains the pool: some repairs need an empty pool, but whether to drain is a call for the repair company. In the City of Yuma, call City of Yuma Utilities at (928) 373-4500 before draining, because city code needs the Director of Utilities' approval to drain a pool into the sewer. The city's stormwater page also says to use the sewer cleanout on your own property, never a public manhole, and never let pool water run into the street.

Cracks, worn plaster and the waterline tile

Plaster and pebble finishes wear out in time, and Angi's resurfacing tips link poor water chemistry to finish damage. Yuma's fill water leans the other way: the City of Yuma rates it hard, at 18 to 22 grains per gallon, and as pool water evaporates the calcium stays behind as a white crust at the water line. The page on pool tile cleaning and calcium scale covers that buildup.

A small crack or a chipped spot can often be patched. A finish that is rough all over, stained through or flaking off may need resurfacing. HomeGuide's resurfacing pages list plaster at about $6 to $8 per square foot, with pebble finishes costing more. Full resurfacing is construction work in Arizona, not a minor repair, so it needs a contractor with a pool construction license.

What "underwater pool repair" means

Most people who search for underwater pool repair simply want to keep the water in the pool. Some fixes allow that. Bob Vila's review of pool patch products notes that certain two-part epoxies and patches are made to cure under water, mostly for small cracks and chips on concrete or plaster. Sealing around a light niche, a return fitting or a skimmer can sometimes be done the same way.

The same review warns that "works underwater" on a label can mean the product survives water once it has cured, not that you can apply it in a full pool. A crack that keeps growing, a shell that has shifted, or a finish failing over a large area needs a drained pool and a proper repair.

Pool lights, drain covers and safety

An underwater light mixes water and electricity, so it is not a job for a homeowner. CPSC says faulty underwater lighting is one of its main electrical concerns, especially in older pools whose fixtures may have worn out or may not have ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection. A GFCI shuts off power when current strays. CPSC advises testing permanently installed GFCIs every month. A homeowner may push the reset button on a tripped GFCI one time. A second trip means the fault is real: leave the circuit off, clear the pool and get a professional.

Drain covers matter just as much. The Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act, signed in December 2007, requires approved drain covers on public pools. For home pools, CPSC says compliant covers are not required but are highly recommended, and that nobody should swim in a pool with a loose, broken or missing cover. Ask the technician to look at yours during any repair visit.

While a pool is damaged or waiting for parts, children should not be near it. Check that the gate swings shut and latches on its own, and keep an adult watching any child in the yard. Among children ages 1 to 4, the CDC says drowning kills more than any other cause.

How a pool repair visit in Yuma usually starts

Expect the first visit to be about finding the cause, before any part is ordered. The technician will likely ask how fast the water drops and when the problem began, then test, look over the fittings, skimmer, light and drain cover, and explain what they found.

Questions worth asking

  • What is causing the problem, and how did you confirm it?
  • Can this be fixed with the pool full, or does it need to be drained?
  • What will the job cost in writing, and what could change that price?
  • Which ROC license do you hold, and may I have the number to look up?
  • Will any part of the job, such as wiring or a gas line, go to another licensed contractor?

Which Arizona license covers which repair

Arizona splits pool work among several Registrar of Contractors classifications. R-6 (Residential Swimming Pool Service and Repair) is the one for routine service and smaller fixes to a home pool and its accessories. Gas piping, wiring past the first electrical disconnect, drinking water plumbing connections and a complete new plaster or pebble interior are carved out of R-6; construction classifications such as B-5 cover pool building and the bigger structural jobs. Arizona's small-job exemption is limited (about $1,000 per project under A.R.S. 32-1121) and never applies when a building permit is needed.

Check the contractor license. Arizona's Registrar of Contractors (ROC) issues the licenses for pool work. Residential R-6, Swimming Pool Service and Repair, is the classification for servicing a home pool and handling minor repairs. Building a new pool or putting in a whole new plaster or pebble surface falls under construction classifications such as B-5. Routine cleaning on its own is a gray area the ROC has not written a clear rule on, so simply ask the company what it holds. Then type its ROC number into the ROC contractor search (new tab) to see if the license is current, what type it is and any recent complaints. Yuma Pool Cleaning Pro does not run this lookup for you.

Common questions

Is my pool leaking or is it just evaporation?

Compare the pool with a bucket. Shut off the pump and the auto fill, fill a bucket with water from the pool, and stand it on the top step with most of its height submerged. Mark the two levels and look again a day later. When the pool has fallen further than the bucket, water is escaping some other way. EPA WaterSense treats a weekly loss above 2 inches, or above 3 inches in hot, dry climates, as a likely leak.

Can a pool be repaired underwater?

Some repairs can. Small cracks, loose fittings and some light niche or skimmer seals can be patched with materials made to cure under water, so the pool stays full. Bigger cracks, structural damage and full resurfacing need the pool drained. Whoever inspects the pool in person is the right person to say which approach fits.

How much does pool repair cost?

Nationally, Angi's 2026 repair price guide puts the typical job near $725 and the usual spread between $243 and $1,212. Finding a leak is priced separately, around $300 on average in Angi's leak detection guide. Treat these as rough national benchmarks. The line sets no prices, and a Yuma company may quote more or less once it sees the pool.

Who can repair a pool in Arizona?

The Arizona Registrar of Contractors (ROC) decides that. Its R-6 classification lets a contractor service home pools and handle smaller fixes. Gas piping, wiring past the first disconnect and a complete new plaster or pebble interior sit outside R-6, so for a full new finish ask which classification the contractor holds; the ROC lists pool building classifications such as B-5 separately. Get the company's ROC number and enter it in the free ROC contractor search before you agree to anything.

Is it safe to swim with a broken pool light or drain cover?

No. CPSC says never to get in a pool or spa with a loose, broken or missing drain cover, and to keep it closed until the cover is fixed. A light that flickers, trips the GFCI or has water inside the lens is an electrical problem. Keep everyone out of the water and have a qualified professional look at it.
